lines.text: An island of ancient tombs, saints and scholars, of conquest, famine and rebellion. This is the story of Ireland, from Newgrange to the modern republic.
More than five thousand years ago, Stone Age farmers raised the great mound of Newgrange, built so the winter sunrise would light its inner chamber.
In the fifth century a missionary named Patrick brought Christianity to Ireland, and became its patron saint.
By around 800, Irish monks were painting the Book of Kells, one of the great treasures of medieval art.
But the Vikings came too. In 841 they built a settlement on the River Liffey, the beginning of Dublin.
Brian Boru, born in the tenth century, rose to be High King of Ireland and challenged the Viking power.
In 1014, at Clontarf, his forces broke the Vikings and their Irish allies, though Brian himself died that day.
Centuries of English rule followed. From 1649 Oliver Cromwell's brutal campaign crushed the power of Catholic Ireland.
In 1667 Jonathan Swift was born, the Dublin clergyman who would write Gulliver's Travels.
In 1690, at the River Boyne, William the Third defeated James the Second, and Protestant rule was secured.
Daniel O'Connell, born in 1775, would be called the Liberator, and win emancipation for Catholics in 1829.
In 1798 the United Irishmen rose against British rule. The rebellion was crushed with terrible loss of life.
Two years later the Act of Union joined Ireland to Great Britain, and its parliament in Dublin was gone.
In 1845 blight destroyed the potato crop. Hundreds of thousands starved, more than a million emigrated, and the island emptied for decades.
In 1854 Oscar Wilde was born in Dublin, the wit behind The Importance of Being Earnest.
W. B. Yeats, the poet who would win the Nobel Prize, was born a decade later.
James Joyce would leave Ireland, yet write of nothing but Dublin, following one day in the city in Ulysses.
That same year Eamon de Valera was born, who would lead Ireland for decades and write its constitution.
Michael Collins would run the rebels' intelligence war, negotiate the treaty with Britain, and die in an ambush.
Samuel Beckett, born in 1906, would write Waiting for Godot and win the Nobel Prize.
In 1915, off the Irish coast, a German submarine sank the liner Lusitania, and many civilians were lost.
At Easter 1916, rebels seized Dublin and declared a republic. They were beaten in days, but the executions turned the country toward independence.
In 1919 a guerrilla war against British rule began, and lasted two years.
In 1922 the Irish Free State was born, and in 1949 it became a republic.
Mary Robinson, born in 1944, would become Ireland's first woman president.
Catherine Connolly, born in 1955, would be elected president seventy years later, in 2025.
From the late sixties, Northern Ireland was torn by thirty years of violence, known as the Troubles.
In 1972, in Derry, British soldiers opened fire on civil rights marchers, killing fourteen.
The next year Ireland joined the European Community, and began to turn outward to Europe.
In 1976 four Dublin teenagers formed U2, who would become one of the biggest bands in the world.
From the mid nineties came the Celtic Tiger, years of growth so fast that Ireland became one of Europe's richest countries.
And in 1998 the Good Friday Agreement brought shared government to the North, approved by voters across the island.
From Newgrange to the Good Friday Agreement, Ireland carries its long memory into a new century.
